content: CD29, also known as integrin beta-1, is a protein encoded by the ITGB1 gene in humans. It is a component of integrin receptors, specifically associated with very late antigen (VLA) receptors. CD29 pairs with the alpha-3 subunit to form the α3β1 complex, which interacts with molecules such as netrin-1 and reelin. In cardiac and skeletal muscle, a specific isoform of integrin beta-1, known as beta-1D, is expressed. This isoform localizes to costameres, where it facilitates the lateral transmission of force from Z-discs to the extracellular matrix. Abnormal levels of integrin beta-1D have been implicated in conditions such as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and polyneuropathy. Integrin beta-1 exists in multiple isoforms due to alternative splicing, with six spliced variants encoding five distinct proteins with different C-terminal regions. Integrin receptors are heterodimers, and more than 20 different integrin heterodimeric receptors have been identified. All integrins, including both alpha and beta subunits, possess large extracellular domains and short intracellular domains. The cytoplasmic domain of integrin beta-1 interacts with the actin cytoskeleton. Among beta-integrins, integrin beta-1 is the most abundantly expressed and associates with at least 10 different alpha subunits. Integrins are transmembrane receptors that mediate cell adhesion and recognition in processes such as embryogenesis, hemostasis, tissue repair, immune responses, and tumor metastasis. They serve as a link between the actin cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix, transmitting signals bidirectionally between these compartments. Beta-integrins, including beta-1, are critical for directing integrin dimers to specific subcellular locations, particularly focal adhesions in adhesive cells. Mutations in integrin beta-1 disrupt its ability to localize to focal adhesions. Three novel isoforms of integrin beta-1 have been identified: beta-1B, beta-1C, and beta-1D. The beta-1B isoform arises from the retention of 26 amino acids in the cytoplasmic domain, followed by a 12-amino-acid sequence from an adjacent intronic region. This isoform acts as a dominant negative, inhibiting cell adhesion. The beta-1C isoform contains an additional 48 amino acids appended to the 26 amino acids in the cytoplasmic domain and inhibits DNA synthesis during the G1 phase of the cell cycle. The beta-1D isoform is specific to striated muscle and replaces the canonical beta-1A isoform in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. It is generated by splicing into a novel exon between exons 6 and 7, resulting in a cytoplasmic domain that replaces the distal 21 amino acids of beta-1A with a unique 24-amino-acid sequence. Beta-1D is developmentally regulated during myofibrillogenesis, appearing after myoblast fusion and increasing in expression during myofibrillar differentiation. It localizes to costameres and intercalated discs in cardiac muscle, as well as costameres, myotendinous junctions, and neuromuscular junctions in skeletal muscle. Functionally, beta-1D integrins resemble other integrins, as their clustering on the surface of CHO cells induces tyrosine phosphorylation of pp125FAK and activates mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. In clinical contexts, integrin beta-1D is significantly reduced in skeletal muscle biopsies from patients with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2C, along with reductions in alpha-7B integrin and filamin 2. Similarly, in patients with sensory-motor polyneuropathy, levels of integrin alpha-7B, integrin beta-1D, and agrin are nearly undetectable, correlating with decreased mRNA expression. CD29 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including ACTN1, CD46, CD9, FHL2, filamin, FLNB, CD81, GNB2L1, ITGB1BP1, LGALS8, MAP4K4, NME1, PKC alpha, TLN1, TSPAN4, and YWHAB. These interactions highlight its diverse roles in cellular processes and signaling pathways.
